name: Chonluten
maker: St Petersburg Institute of Bioregulation and Gerontology (V. Khavinson)

overview.headline: A three-amino-acid peptide sold for the lungs, though its inventors patented it as a stress-protective agent. One short Russian study in healthy volunteers.
overview.lede: Chonluten is the Khavinson institute's tripeptide Glu-Asp-Gly. Vendors sell it for the lungs; the institute's U.S. patent (2011) describes a stress protector acting on brain chemistry, a European patent covers Helicobacter stomach disease, and a 2020 review mentions chronic bronchitis. It is not a registered medicine anywhere.

stats.lbl: healthy men aged 20–22 in the only human study, a two-day altitude-tolerance test
controlled studies in people with lung disease
stats.src: PubMed, patents, institute publications and registries, Oct 2026

mechanism.intro: A short peptide said to steady the stress response and protect mucous membranes.

parts.name: The bioregulator idea
parts.text: The 2016 computer model places Chonluten on the DNA sequence "tttt" with only "weak" predicted binding, the lowest grade in the institute's table.

parts.name: What the animal work showed
parts.text: In the patent, rats given the peptide for five days had more noradrenaline, dopamine and serotonin in the brain cortex and less in blood, and the stress gene c-Fos changed in stressed rats. The bronchitis claim rests on one sentence in a review; the group's bronchial cell paper tested Bronchogen, not Chonluten.

more.title: More: three stories for one peptide
paras: Vendors: lungs. U.S. patent: stress protection and altitude tolerance. European patent EP 2667887: Helicobacter-related stomach disease. Institute review: chronic bronchitis. None has been shown in a controlled human study.

results.headline: Rat brain chemistry, one two-day volunteer study, and a bronchitis claim without data.
results.lede: The only human data come from 80 healthy young men who sat in a low-pressure chamber for an hour after two days of the peptide or placebo.

stats.lbl: volunteers who tolerated simulated 5,000 m altitude well, peptide versus placebo; blinding not described

items.t: Serum from five donors: the peptide inhibited enkephalin-degrading enzymes about as well as two reference inhibitors; figure only (patent).

27 rats: brain-cortex noradrenaline, dopamine and serotonin up after five days. 28 rats under restraint stress: c-Fos changes in the hypothalamus. Toxicity tests in 66 mice, 64 rats and 92 guinea pigs: no toxic reactions. Not in a journal.

80 healthy men (20 placebo, 30 and 30 on the peptide) spent an hour at simulated 5,000 m: 80–90% tolerated it well versus 60%; anxiety scores 10–13% lower; work capacity 15–20% higher. Randomisation and blinding not described. The bronchitis statement has no reference, numbers or design.

more.title: More: why the volunteer study says nothing about lungs
paras: Tolerating thin air for an hour is a stress-physiology outcome in fit young men, not a lung-disease outcome in patients, and the percentages come from an unreviewed patent.

effects.headline: No patient safety data. Eighty volunteers for two days, and rodent toxicity tests in a patent.
effects.lede: The volunteer study reports no adverse events but was not designed to find them. Rodent testing reported no toxic reactions.

disc.title: Stopping because of side effects
disc.text: Not measurable: no trial has been run.

unique.title: What is actually known
unique.text: Almost nothing. In rats the peptide changed brain levels of noradrenaline, dopamine and serotonin, the chemicals mood and blood-pressure drugs act on. What that means in a person is unmeasured.

more.title: More: what a trial would monitor for
paras: Mood, sleep, heart rate and blood pressure, given the brain-amine changes in rats; lung function if the bronchitis claim were tested; immune reactions.

more.title: More: the good side effects
paras: In rats: changed brain chemistry under stress. In 80 young men: better tolerance of an hour of simulated altitude, by the inventors' account. In lung patients: nothing measured.

urgent.title: Symptoms a doctor should see promptly
items: Spreading redness, swelling or pus at an injection site, or fever and chills after an injection
Hives, swelling of the face or throat, trouble breathing
Yellowing of the skin or eyes, dark urine
urgent.note: No trial has defined this peptide's own danger signs; these relate to an unverified product.

levels.nopk: No one has measured Chonluten in a person's blood; no half-life or absorption figure exists for it in any species. There is nothing to build a curve from.

stats.lbl: length of the only human exposure on record, in healthy volunteers

explain.t: The simulator on other pages needs a measured half-life; none exists for Chonluten.

explain.b: Why the oral claim is contested.
explain.t: Pharmacologists expect peptides this short to be digested by gut and blood enzymes; the institute says they are absorbed intact. Nothing in people settles it.

more.title: More: what this page cannot tell you
paras: What is in a product sold as Chonluten, or what repeated use does: no independent analysis exists, and no study has followed anyone beyond a few weeks.

trials.headline: One unregistered volunteer study in a patent. No trial in patients.
trials.lede: No trial in people with lung disease, stress disorders or stomach disease has been published or registered.

more.title: More: how the volunteer study was run
paras: Eighty men aged 20–22 were split into a placebo group of 20 and two peptide groups of 30, took the peptide or placebo for two days, and on day four sat for 60 minutes in a pressure chamber set to 5,000 metres while anxiety, heart rate, blood pressure and work capacity were recorded. Assignment and blinding are not described.

running.title: Trials that have been run
items: Altitude-tolerance study, 80 healthy men, two days (patent, 2011): better tolerance and lower anxiety reported; design details missing; not peer reviewed.
Chronic bronchitis: mentioned in a 2020 institute review, with no study cited.
No trial on ClinicalTrials.gov or any registry we could find (October 2026).

find.text: Search the registry for "Chonluten" and its sequence "EDG". We found no registered trial.

status.headline: Not approved anywhere. A "research chemical" with three competing marketing stories.

items.label: Canada
items.text: Never authorised by Health Canada as a medicine or natural health product (October 2026).

items.label: United States
items.text: Not FDA-approved; absent from FDA's 503A compounding category list of 14 May 2026.

items.label: Russia
items.text: Not a registered medicine; not among the institute's six licensed products, and no Russian registration of any kind found.

cards.title: What a "bioregulator" claim rests on
cards.text: The claim is that a peptide copied from an organ extract reaches that organ and switches on its genes. For Chonluten the support is:
items: Computer docking models, test-tube DNA work and cell cultures from one institute; no study has tracked one of these peptides into a human organ.
Chonluten is the weakest DNA binder in the institute's own model, and its patents describe a stress protector and a stomach treatment, not a lung peptide.

cards.title: What "research use only" means
cards.text: A "research use only" label is a legal device, not a safety rating. No regulator in Canada or the U.S. has checked what is in a vial sold as Chonluten, and no toxicology or purity data have been filed in the West.
items: Whether a supplement under the name Хонлутен is currently registered in Russia we could not confirm.

cards.title: Symptoms to take to a doctor
cards.text: If any of these appear after using such a product, see a doctor and bring the product:
items: Fever, chills, or a hot, swollen injection site
Hives, swelling of the face or throat, trouble breathing
Yellowing of the skin or eyes, dark urine
cards.note: Report a reaction to MedEffect Canada (canada.ca/medeffect) or, in the U.S., FDA MedWatch (fda.gov/medwatch).

more.title: More: the Khavinson peptide family
paras: Vladimir Khavinson (1946–2024) directed the St Petersburg Institute of Bioregulation and Gerontology, which made animal-organ extracts from the 1970s and then designed two- to four-amino-acid peptides from each extract's amino-acid make-up, naming them after target organs. Six products became licensed medicines in the USSR or Russia: Thymalin (1982), Thymogen and Epithalamin (1990), Prostatilen (1992), Cortexin and Retinalamin (1999). The synthetic organ-named peptides sold online are not among them, and none appears in an international trial registry.
